strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical task, RGBA text-to-video generation, which has substantial utility in video editing, gaming, and creative content creation.

The proposed VAE architecture utilizes a 3D causal feature merging block and LoRA/DoRA adapters, making it parameter-efficient and easy to integrate with the base model without extra inference overhead.
The qualitative results demonstrate strong performance in capturing fine-grained transparent details like hair, complex edges, and glowing effects.
The inference pipeline is highly optimized, demonstrating a 15x speedup compared to TransPixeler by utilizing a distilled 4-step sampling strategy without classifier-free guidance.
weaknesses: The evaluation is purely qualitative. The paper lacks quantitative comparisons (such as FVD, CLIP score, or quantitative alpha-channel precision metrics like MSE or SAD) with baseline methods like TransPixeler.

A thorough ablation study is missing. It is unclear how much each component contributes to the final performance, such as the causal 3D merge block vs. simpler concatenation, the impact of the specific loss functions (e.g., Sobel edge loss), or the choice of DoRA over LoRA.

The text-to-video training set is extremely small, consisting of only 437 samples. This raises concerns about the generalization capability of the model on open-domain text prompts, as it may easily overfit to the limited training concepts.

A user study or human evaluation is missing. Given that transparency and visual quality are highly subjective, a structured user preference study comparing the proposed model with TransPixeler would significantly strengthen the claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and relatively under-explored task: high-quality text-to-video generation with transparency (RGBA), which has broad applications in gaming, video editing, and AR/VR.

High inference efficiency: Unlike existing methods like TransPixeler that double the backbone and introduce heavy cross-attention (which doubles inference cost), Wan-Alpha merges the LoRA/DoRA weights directly into the base model. This results in zero extra computational overhead at inference time, achieving a massive 15x speedup (128 seconds vs. 32 minutes) on the same hardware.

The architecture design is clean and logical. Introducing a causal 3D convolutional feature merge block in the VAE, combined with hard/soft rendering pipelines and multi-component losses (reconstruction, perceptual, and Sobel edge losses), successfully handles fine-grained details (like hair strands) and complex semi-transparent/glow effects.
Excellent qualitative results: The visual comparisons against TransPixeler (both open and closed versions) show superior edge sharpness, better temporal consistency, and fewer artifacts.
weaknesses: Lack of quantitative evaluation: The evaluation is entirely qualitative and visual. The paper would be significantly stronger with quantitative metrics assessing video quality (e.g., FVD), semantic alignment (e.g., CLIP score), and temporal consistency, as well as VAE reconstruction accuracy (e.g., PSNR, SSIM, or standard matting metrics like MSE/SAD).

Limited training dataset size for text-to-video: The fine-tuning dataset for text-to-video contains only 437 samples (301 videos, 20 images, 116 special effects). While highly curated, such a small dataset might limit the generalization capabilities of the model to diverse or out-of-distribution textual prompts.

The conceptual novelty is somewhat moderate, as the core philosophy of embedding the alpha channel into the RGB latent space is closely aligned with prior works like LayerDiffuse and AlphaVAE, adapted here for the video domain using standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA/DoRA).

strengths: Practical and high-utility task: Transparent video (RGBA) generation is of great importance for video editing, AR/VR, and game design.

Highly efficient design: By mapping the alpha channel into the existing latent space and using LoRA/DoRA, the method avoids duplicating the backbone DiT network, preserving the inference efficiency of the original model.
Excellent qualitative results: The generated videos show impressive handling of difficult transparent cases, such as hair strands, glowing effects, and semi-transparent liquids.
Very fast inference: Achieving 15x faster generation compared to TransPixeler by leveraging LightX2V and 4-step inference without CFG.
weaknesses: Lack of quantitative evaluation: The paper relies entirely on qualitative visual comparisons. Standard metrics for video generation (e.g., FVD, CLIP score for text alignment) or segmentation/matting quality metrics of the generated alpha channel are missing. A user study (human evaluation) would also strengthen the paper.

Extremely small fine-tuning dataset: The text-to-video dataset contains only 437 samples. While high-quality, this very small size raises concerns about the model's ability to generalize to diverse, unseen prompts.

Confounding factors in the baseline comparison: The baseline TransPixeler is built on CogVideoX-5B, whereas Wan-Alpha is built on the newer Wan model. It is difficult to decouple how much of the improvement in visual quality and speed comes from the proposed RGBA training strategy versus the inherently stronger and faster Wan base model.

Incremental technical novelty: Combining a feature merge block, dual decoders with LoRA, and training with standard rendering losses is largely an extension of LayerDiffuse/AlphaVAE concepts to the video domain.

strengths: Well-designed Dual-space Adjustment: Modifying both the latent space (via VAE training with bidirectional loss) and the noise space (via mean-shifted noise sampling) is a comprehensive approach to disentangling RGB and alpha channels without compromising RGB quality.

Inference Efficiency: By utilizing LoRA/DoRA and avoiding backbone duplication (unlike TransPixeler), the model retains the base model's speed and compatibility with acceleration tools (e.g., LightX2V), achieving 15x faster generation speed.

Explicit Transparency Control: The mean-shifted noise sampler provides an intuitive and controllable spatial prior over the foreground object's position and scale during inference without requiring additional conditional networks.

Strong Quantitative and Qualitative Results: Demonstrates clear improvements over existing baselines (LayerFlow, TransPixeler, etc.) in both automated metrics (VBench, GPT-4o) and user studies, producing high-fidelity semi-transparent details like hair and smoke.
weaknesses: Training Stability of Bidirectional Loss: In Equation 3, the loss is defined as $L_{bidiff} = M \cdot L_{RF}$, where $M(p) = -1$ for transparent regions. Minimizing a negative loss is equivalent to maximizing the matching error (gradient ascent). This can easily lead to instability, exploding gradients, or out-of-distribution latent values. The authors should discuss how training stability is ensured under this formulation.

Limitations of Single Gaussian Ellipse Representative: The transparency-guided mean sampler fits a single Gaussian ellipse to the alpha mask. While this works well for a single centered foreground object, it may fail to represent complex scenes with multiple disjoint objects or highly irregular shapes.

Inference Mask Specification: For text-to-video generation, how is the ellipse mask designed if the user does not provide one? If the default is simply centered, does the model struggle to generate off-center or multi-object scenes as dictated by more complex prompts?

Dataset Scale: The fine-tuning dataset for video generation consists of only 429 samples. Fine-tuning a massive 14B parameter model (Wan2.1) on such a small dataset risks overfitting and might reduce the model's general open-domain generation capabilities.

strengths: Novel and Elegant Formulation: The paper proposes an elegant solution to the entanglement of RGB and Alpha channels. Shifting the alpha distribution while preserving the RGB distribution in both the latent space (via TABD loss) and noise space (via TGMS) is highly intuitive and technically sound.

Innovative VAE Training: The Transparency-Aware Bidirectional Diffusion (TABD) loss is a clever design. By utilizing a frozen DiT during VAE training and inverting the diffusion loss in transparent regions, the VAE is incentivized to produce latents that the generator can easily differentiate, successfully preventing common artifacts like 'holes' in opaque regions.

Controllable Generation: The transparency-guided mean sampler (TGMS) not only guides the model during training but also provides an intuitive inference-time control mechanism (shape and position) using a simple Gaussian ellipse mask without sacrificing fine-grained details or visual naturalness.

Impressive Performance and Efficiency: The model shows clear qualitative and quantitative improvements over state-of-the-art baselines like TransPixeler and LayerFlow. Notably, it is extremely efficient, achieving a 15x speedup during inference compared to TransPixeler, making it highly practical.
Comprehensive Evaluation: The paper presents a thorough quantitative evaluation (using VBench and GPT-4o), a detailed user study, and a clear ablation study validating all key design choices.
weaknesses: Limitation of Single Ellipse Mask: The mean-shifting strategy relies on a single Gaussian ellipse fitted to the binarized alpha mask. While this works well for single-subject videos, it is unclear how the method handles scenes with multiple disconnected transparent/opaque subjects (e.g., two separate characters moving independently) where a single ellipse might cover a large empty center.

Sensitivity of Color Rendering Set: For the VAE reconstruction, a predefined color set C is used to randomly render background colors. The paper would be stronger if it included a discussion on the sensitivity of the VAE performance to this set (e.g., if highly complex background patterns instead of solid colors were used).

Details on Dataset Collection: The paper mentions converting 77k images into static videos for training the VAE, but the DiT generation training dataset seems much smaller (approx. 429 samples). More details on how this size disparity affects the generalization capability of the video generator on unseen text prompts or categories would be helpful.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and challenging task: RGB-A (transparent) video generation, which has significant applications in game development, VFX, and UI design.

The proposed Transparency-Aware Bidirectional Diffusion Loss (TABD) is a creative way to leverage a frozen pre-trained DiT to guide the latent space of the VAE, helping to disentangle RGB and alpha distributions.
The Transparency-Guided Mean Sampler (TGMS) provides an elegant mechanism for both stable training and user-controllable spatial layout of the transparency channel at inference time.
The paper is well-written, with high-quality visual results, clear formulations, and a solid suite of comparisons against existing approaches like TransPixeler and LayerFlow.
weaknesses: Mathematical instability of the bidirectional loss: In Equation 3, the mask $M(p)$ takes a negative value (-1) in transparent/semi-transparent regions. This effectively reverses the gradient to maximize the rectified flow loss in these regions. Maximizing a loss function is mathematically unstable and can lead to exploding gradients or latent representation collapse. The manuscript does not discuss how this training instability is avoided (e.g., via gradient clipping, margins, or balancing weights).

Small dataset size for video generation tuning: The video generation dataset consists of only around 429 samples (301 videos, 43 images, 85 special effects videos). While the base model (Wan2.1) is large and capable, fine-tuning on such a small dataset can lead to overfitting or a significant loss of the base model's general capability and concept vocabulary. An evaluation of the model's concept retention or open-world generation capability after tuning is missing.

Limitations of the Gaussian ellipse mask ($G$): The mean-shifting mechanism relies on fitting a single Gaussian ellipse. During inference, $G$ is placed in the center by default. It remains unclear how the model behaves when generating multiple distinct objects, or complex shapes that cannot be approximated by a single ellipse. This assumption might restrict the spatial composition diversity of the generated videos.

Lack of objective quantitative evaluation for the alpha channel: In Table 1, the quantitative evaluations (VBench, GPT-4o) assess standard video quality metrics on a white background but do not directly measure the precision of the alpha channel. While a user study is provided, the paper would be significantly stronger if it evaluated the generated alpha channels against a ground-truth test set using standard matting metrics (e.g., Mean Absolute Difference, MSE, or Connectivity L1 loss).
